newsitem.title: USA: Emotions high in Miami over hurricane aid for Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Emotions high in Miami over hurricane aid for Cuba.

text.p: With thousands of their countrymen left homeless by Hurricane Lili, Cuban exiles in Florida hotly debated on Monday whether to send aid, fearing their charity might help Cuba's Communist regime.

The hurricane, which swept through central and western Cuba on Thursday and Friday, destroyed 5,640 homes and damaged another 84,000, Cuban offials said. It also caused extensive damage to crops. No deaths were reported.

The disaster affected the estimated one million Cubans and Cuban-Americans living in southern Florida, virtually all of whom still have close relatives on the island but are fierce opponents of President Fidel Castro's government.
Radio programmes were instantly flooded with appeals for humanitarian aid along with calls not to send any assistance.

"We are against sending anything to Cuba because we have the experience when another storm hit Cuba before, all the help that the government received, that help didn't go to the people of Cuba. It went to the government of Cuba," said Tomas Garcia-Fuste, programming director at WCMQ, a radio station leading the drive against sending aid.

"The solution for us is not to give to the people of Cuba charity. It is not charity what they need, what they need is that government that we have for 38 years in January, finished," he said, adding that the station had received thousands of telephone calls and faxes supporting its stance.

But the appeals to hold off on aid seemed to have fallen on deaf ears in Miami's large Cuban-American community. By mid-day, more than 150,000 pounds (68,000 kg) of donated food and other goods including more than 50,000 pounds (23,000 kg) of rice were amassed at a Catholic Relief Services warehouse and the Archdiocese of Miami said far more was expected.
"There's a lot of stuff out in the parishes that hasn't come in," said the Rev. Thomas Wenski, director of Catholic Charities for the archidiocese.

"We just want to help our brothers and sisters who are in such a disaster," said Lucy Brena, assistant producer at WQBA, a radio station known for its normally hardline anti-Castro stance that nonetheless conducted a marathon drive for donations in the days after Lili made landfall in Cuba.

Experts said they were not surprised at the amount of aid offered -- offers of passage on ships and planes as well as an unknown amount of cash donations came along with the goods provided -- or at the extent of the controversy.

"I'm not surprised that there's a difference of opinion on that," said Lisandro Perez, director of the Cuban Research Institute at Florida International University in Miami. "There's always been this notion, founded or unfounded, in the Cuban community, that the humanitarian aid does not really get to the people, that it's appropriated by the government."

But Perez said Caritas, the Catholic relief organisation, had a good record of taking medical aid to the people in Cuba. "I know that because I've talked to people at the parish level in Cuba ... that receive medicines and distribute it themselves," he said.

Wenski said opponents of the aid might not be aware of the track record Caritas had established, noting Catholic Relief Services has sent about $8 million worth of medicine and other supplies to the island in the past three years.

But any shipment would have to wait for receipt of special licenses from the U.S. government, which -- at the urging of Miami's hardline Cuban exiles -- passed tough new laws against trade with Cuba this year.
Peter Coats, a Catholic relief worker at the Miami warehouse, also noted that Caritas must send an inventory to the Cuban government and win its approval for any shipment.
